from.place: Proof paragraph 2, finite coefficient mapping-complex adjunction before R lim; supporting the enriched tensor/localization calculus: Lemma 5.1.2, Proposition 5.1.15, Corollaries 5.2.7 and 5.2.10, Lemmas 5.3.2, 5.3.4 and 5.3.5, Proposition 5.3.6; Lemma A.5.5

title: Equivalence nerves and detection of fully faithful equivalences
statement: Let $\mathcal V$ be presentably monoidal, and use the algebroids of [def-coef-complete-algebroid]. For an algebroid $C$ with object space $U(C)$, put $I_n(C)=\operatorname{Map}(E^n,C)$ and $I(C)=|I_\bullet(C)|$, the geometric realization in spaces. The finite sets $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ with their usual maps make $E^\bullet$ cosimplicial and $I_\bullet(C)$ simplicial. For a nonempty ordered subset $S\subseteq[n]$, write $I_S(C)=I_{|S|-1}(C)$, with restriction maps induced by its increasing enumeration. There is a natural identification $I_0(C)\simeq U(C)$. The simplicial space $I_\bullet(C)$ is a groupoid object: for every union $[n]=S\cup T$ of ordered subsets meeting in one vertex, restriction identifies $I_n(C)$ with $I_S(C)\times_{I_{S\cap T}(C)}I_T(C)$. The algebroid $C$ is complete if and only if $U(C)\to I(C)$ is an equivalence. A fully faithful $F:C\to D$ induces equivalences on the fibers of $I_1(C)\to U(C)^2$ over $(x,y)$ and $I_1(D)\to U(D)^2$ over $(Fx,Fy)$. An element of the fiber $I_1(C)_{x,y}$ is an equivalence from $x$ to $y$; this fiber identifies with the union of invertible components in $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))$. A functor is essentially surjective if and only if every target object is equivalent to an image object, or equivalently if $\pi_0 I(F)$ is surjective. If it is also fully faithful, then $I(F)$ is an equivalence. A fully faithful algebroid map whose map on object spaces is an equivalence is an equivalence in $\operatorname{Algd}(\mathcal V)$. Composition on either side with an equivalence between objects induces equivalences of enriched mapping objects. All these statements are natural in algebroid maps.

source.place: Lemma 5.1.2, Propositions 5.1.15 and 5.1.17, Corollaries 5.2.7 and 5.2.10, Lemmas 5.3.2, 5.3.4 and 5.3.5, Proposition 5.3.6; Lemma A.5.5 (read online; not archived in literature/). No Stacks tag states this infinity-categorical fact.

proof.text: The finite-set algebroids $E^n$ and their maps are defined in [def-coef-complete-algebroid]. Precomposition reverses the cosimplicial operators and gives the stated simplicial space. The definition of completeness there is exactly that $I_0(C)\to|I_\bullet(C)|$ is an equivalence. Step 3 will identify its evaluation map $I_0(C)\to U(C)$ naturally as an equivalence, which then gives the asserted completeness criterion.

Reduce the enriched calculations to spaces as follows. At the terminal monoidal category, [lem-coef-algebroid-segal-localization-model] states that $\mathcal S=P(*)$ is presentably monoidal and that cartesian product preserves small colimits separately. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-presheaf-free-cocompletion] with the terminal category: its presheaf category is $\mathcal S$, so the object $\mathbf1\in\mathcal V$ extends to the colimit-preserving functor $T(K)=\operatorname{colim}_K\mathbf1$. The mapping-space colimit criterion of [lem-coef-infinity-yoneda-presheaf-limits] gives $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(T(K),v)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal S}(K,\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,v))$. Thus $T\dashv R$ with $R(v)=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,v)$. Separate preservation of colimits by tensor gives $T(K)\otimes T(L)\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{K\times L}(\mathbf1\otimes\mathbf1)\simeq T(K\times L)$ and $T(*)\simeq\mathbf1$. For coherence, apply the free-cocompletion equivalence successively in each variable: restriction of separately colimit-preserving functors $\mathcal S^r\to\mathcal V$ to the tuple $(*,\ldots,*)$ is fully faithful, including transformations and higher simplices. Both sides of every iterated tensor comparison preserve colimits separately. Thus the unit constraints on $\mathbf1$ extend uniquely up to contractible choice to these comparisons, and the associativity, unit diagrams and their higher compatibilities extend along the same fully faithful restrictions. The displayed comparison is an equivalence because its restriction is the unit-constraint equivalence; this also follows directly from the displayed colimit calculation. Construct the required enriched mapping adjunction without appealing to completion. Postcomposition with the strong monoidal $T$ and its adjoint lax monoidal $R$ gives $T_*$ and $R_*$, with $R_*C(x,y)=R(C(x,y))$ and unchanged object spaces. First construct the object-space mapping formula independently of equivalence nerves. The total category in [def-coef-complete-algebroid] is the Grothendieck construction of $X\mapsto\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal V)$, with pullback given by precomposition. Enlarge the ambient universe to contain the category of original-small spaces and all its algebra fibers, and enlarge once more to form their category of fibrations; the object spaces themselves stay original-small. Apply [lem-coef-cocartesian-straightening] to $X\mapsto\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal V)^{\mathrm{op}}$ over $\mathcal S^{\mathrm{op}}$, then take opposites. This identifies the defined total category with a Cartesian fibration, whose Cartesian lift of $\phi:X\to Y$ with target $B$ is $\phi^*B\to B$, represented by the identity of $\phi^*B$. The $K=\Delta^0$ case of [lem-coef-infinity-pointwise-cocartesian-transport], applied to its opposite, gives the mapping-space fiber formula. The construction applies to both $\mathcal V$ and $\mathcal S$, and is natural under coefficient postcomposition since this commutes with restriction. For algebroids $A$ over $X$ and $B$ over $Y$, this formula identifies the fibers of $\operatorname{Map}(T_*A,B)$ and $\operatorname{Map}(A,R_*B)$ over $\phi:X\to Y$ with $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal V)}(T_*A,\phi^*B)$ and $\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Alg}_X(\mathcal S)}(A,R_*\phi^*B)$. By [lem-coef-many-object-operad-accessibility], restriction along $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}\to q(X)=L_{\mathrm{gen}}\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$ identifies these algebra categories naturally with algebras over the small ordinary nonsymmetric operad $q(X)$. Apply [lem-coef-operadic-change-enrichment] to $T\dashv R$ and this operad. It supplies natural equivalences of the displayed fibers, commuting coherently with restriction in $X$ and with the units and counits. Explicitly, the forward map sends $k$ to $R_*(k)\eta_A$, and its inverse sends $h$ to $\varepsilon_B T_*(h)$; they preserve the object-space map $\phi$, since the algebra unit and counit fix the object space. The restriction compatibility makes these maps defined on the total mapping spaces over $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal S}(X,Y)$, with all higher simplices. Over the identity of this base their fibers are equivalences, so [lem-coef-spaces-homotopy-fiber-detection] gives the equivalence of total mapping spaces, naturally in $A,B$. This is precisely the mapping-space adjunction required here. Since $T(*)=\mathbf1$, it sends each coarse space-enriched algebroid $E_A^{\mathcal S}$ to $E_A^{\mathcal V}$. Therefore, naturally in finite sets $A$ and algebroids $C$,
$$\operatorname{Map}(E_A^{\mathcal V},C)\simeq\operatorname{Map}(E_A^{\mathcal S},R_*C).$$

source.place: Example 4.3.20, Definition 5.1.10 and Proposition 5.1.11; the strong monoidal structure is checked by the displayed colimit calculation.; ordinary-operadic mapping adjunction: Proposition A.5.11, with Lemma 4.3.19 for assembly over object spaces; Cartesian straightening and its opposite mapping-fiber formula, HTT 3.2.0.1 and 2.4.4.2, with ambient-universe enlargement

proof.text: In [lem-coef-algebroid-segal-localization-model], take the small monoidal category to be the terminal category and take the coefficient localization set empty. Then $P(*)=\mathcal S$, its Day tensor is cartesian product (both sides at the only object are the product of values), and $Q_*$ is the full category of Segal spaces. The stated equivalence identifies $R_*C$ with a Segal space $W_C$, with $(W_C)_0=U(C)$ and $(W_C)(x,y)=\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))$. Under this same explicit object-and-mapping-object identification, $E_A^{\mathcal S}$ has $(n+1)$-tuples of objects $A^{n+1}$ in degree $n$, with the uniquely prescribed composites: it is $dG_A$ for $G_A=N(\mathcal I_A)$. Full faithfulness of that equivalence now turns Step 2 into $\operatorname{Map}(E_A^{\mathcal V},C)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal P_\Delta}(dG_A,W_C)$. These equivalences respect every finite-set map, evaluation on edges, units and composition. For a singleton $A$, $dG_A$ is the constant point simplicial space, which is the free diagram $[0]!*$ on $[0]\in\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$, since there is exactly one map $[n]\to[0]$ in $\Delta$. The free-diagram mapping equivalence in [lem-coef-coherent-diagram-coyoneda], with $I=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $\mathcal B=\mathcal S$, gives $\operatorname{Map}(dG_A,W_C)\simeq\operatorname{Map}(*,(W_C)_0)\simeq U(C)$. Its map is evaluation at that vertex. Hence $I_0(C)\simeq U(C)$ naturally; applying the Step 1 definition proves the completeness assertion.

source.place: Theorem 4.4.7; the explicit identification of coarse algebras in the proof of Theorem 5.2.5.; evaluation by the free-diagram adjunction (relative Yoneda)

proof.text:
Fix finite sets $A$, $a\in A$ and $b\notin A$. By [lem-coef-coarse-nerve-gluing] the inclusion $G_A\amalg_{G_a}G_{\{a,b\}}\to G_{A\cup\{b\}}$ is inner anodyne. Here inner-anodyne maps induce mapping-space equivalences into $W_C$ by the following induction, using [lem-coef-labelled-spine-prism-horn-calculus] at terminal coefficients. By the free-diagram equivalence of [lem-coef-coherent-diagram-coyoneda] with $I=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ and $\mathcal B=\mathcal S$, $d\Delta^n=[n]!*$ since $\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([k],[n])=(\Delta^n)_k$, so $\operatorname{Map}(d\Delta^n,W_C)\simeq(W_C)_n$ by evaluation; with the pointwise-colimit criterion used below, mapping the spine (glued from $d\Delta^1$ along $d\Delta^0$ by injections) into $W_C$ gives $(W_C)_1\times_{(W_C)_0}\cdots\times_{(W_C)_0}(W_C)_1$. In dimension two the inner horn is the spine. In dimension $m>2$, the spine-to-inner-horn inclusion is a finite composite of pushouts of inner horns of dimensions less than $m$, so by induction its restriction on mapping spaces is an equivalence. The spine-to-simplex restriction is an equivalence by the Segal condition; two-out-of-three therefore proves the inner-horn-to-simplex restriction is an equivalence. The same conclusion is closed under pushouts, transfinite compositions and retracts: a pushout along a degreewise injection is a homotopy pushout after passage from sets to discrete spaces (in each degree, the graph presenting the pushout has a tree as each component), and an increasing transfinite union is its homotopy colimit. By [lem-coef-infinity-yoneda-presheaf-limits], these colimits are pointwise and mapping out turns them into limits; limits and retracts of equivalences are equivalences. Thus mapping the coarse inclusion above into $W_C$ gives an equivalence, with no extra locality prerequisite. The displayed pushout remains a pushout in simplicial spaces: it is pointwise a pushout of discrete sets along injections, hence also a homotopy pushout (its components are trees with contractible realizations). Pointwise computation and conversion of a colimit to a limit under contravariant representables are supplied by [lem-coef-infinity-yoneda-presheaf-limits]. Hence
$$\operatorname{Map}(dG_{A\cup\{b\}},W_C)\simeq\operatorname{Map}(dG_A,W_C)\times_{(W_C)_0}\operatorname{Map}(dG_{\{a,b\}},W_C).$$
For $[n]=S\cup T$ with $S\cap T=\{a\}$, list the vertices of $T\setminus\{a\}$. Induct on their number, starting with $T=\{a\}$ where restriction is the identity. The displayed one-vertex attachment formula successively identifies the restriction for $S\cup T$ with $\operatorname{Map}(dG_S,W_C)$ times, over the common vertex, one two-object factor for each listed vertex. Applying the same attachments starting from $\{a\}$ identifies that product of two-object factors with $\operatorname{Map}(dG_T,W_C)$. Associativity of the pullback therefore gives exactly the claimed $I_S(C)\times_{I_{S\cap T}(C)}I_T(C)$. Coarse nerves admit all permutations of their labels, so the pivot need not be an endpoint of the increasing ordering. The comparison itself is the original restriction map; the temporary enumeration is used only to prove it is an equivalence.

source.place: Theorem 5.2.5 and Corollary 5.2.7: elementary-attachment induction; the Segal-locality argument uses the terminal specialization of the cited lower-dimensional spine-to-horn filtration. The lower-dimensional induction follows Haugseng, On the tensor product of enriched infinity-categories, arXiv:2311.13362v1, Corollaries 6.5 and 6.6.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-segal-inverse-evaluation] to $W_C$. The two-object coarse nerve $G_{\{0,1\}}$ in Step 3 is its walking isomorphism $E$, so evaluation gives $I_1(C)\simeq(W_C)_{\mathrm{inv}}$ over $U(C)^2$. Pull back over $(x,y)$ and use Step 3's identification of the mapping space to obtain the stated union of invertible components of $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal V}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))$. A map $E^1\to C$ together with identifications of its endpoints with $(x,y)$ is exactly a point of this homotopy fiber; these endpoint identifications are paths, not strict equalities. Under the coefficient adjunction and Segal comparison, its edge is a map $\mathbf1\to C(x,y)$ invertible in $hW_C$, hence admitting a reverse arrow and both unit homotopies. Conversely Rezk evaluation says that every such invertible edge extends through $E^1$ with a contractible space of coherent choices. Thus these are precisely object equivalences in the enriched category. This proves the assertion for the whole fiber space, not merely a bijection on its components.

source.place: Theorem 6.2, with the invertible-arrow subspace of Sections 5.5 and 5.7; the enriched application is Gepner-Haugseng Propositions 5.1.15 and 5.1.17.

proof.text: Let $F:C\to D$ be fully faithful. Its mapping-object equivalences induce equivalences of spaces $H_C(x,y)=\operatorname{Map}(\mathbf1,C(x,y))\simeq H_D(Fx,Fy)$. They preserve units and compositions, so they preserve invertibility. Conversely, if the image of $\alpha\in H_C(x,y)$ has an inverse, lift this inverse to $\beta\in H_C(y,x)$. The equations for its two composites lift on components through the equivalences $H_C(x,x)\simeq H_D(Fx,Fx)$ and $H_C(y,y)\simeq H_D(Fy,Fy)$, giving $\beta\alpha=1_x$ and $\alpha\beta=1_y$ in the homotopy category. Thus $F$ reflects invertibility as well. Restricting an equivalence of spaces to the corresponding unions of components is an equivalence (it restricts the bijection on components and retains every based homotopy group). Step 5 identifies these restrictions with exactly the required maps on $I_1$ fibers.

source.place: Lemma 5.3.5, with reflection of invertibility checked by lifting a two-sided inverse.

proof.text: By Step 4 and [lem-coef-space-geometric-descent], $I_\bullet(C)$ and $I_\bullet(D)$ are effective groupoids. Thus $U(C)\to I(C)$ and $U(D)\to I(D)$ are surjective on components, and $I_1(D)\simeq U(D)\times_{I(D)}U(D)$. If every object of $D$ is equivalent to an image, each component of $I(D)$ consequently meets the image of $I(C)$. Conversely, if $\pi_0I(F)$ is surjective, lift any target component first to $U(C)$ using its surjection on components. Equality of its image with the component of an object $d$ means a path in $I(D)$ from that image to $d$; effectivity identifies this path with a point of the corresponding $I_1(D)$ fiber, hence with an object equivalence by Step 5. This proves the equivalence between the two formulations; [def-coef-complete-algebroid] defines essential surjectivity by the component formulation.

source.place: Lemma 5.3.4, with the quotient argument expressed using effectivity.

proof.text: Put $A=I(C)$, $B=I(D)$ and $f=I(F)$. Effectivity identifies the path spaces of $A$ between points of $U(C)$ with the corresponding fibers of $I_1(C)$, and similarly for $B$. Hence Step 6 gives equivalences on these path spaces. Apply the final descent criterion of [lem-coef-space-geometric-descent] to the square with top row $A\xrightarrow{f}B$ and bottom row $A\times A\xrightarrow{f\times f}B\times B$, whose vertical maps are diagonals. The map $U(C)^2\to A^2$ is surjective on components; over any of its points the fiber comparison is exactly the path-space equivalence just proved. Descent therefore makes its comparison $A\to A\times_B A$ an equivalence. For any $b\in B$, the homotopy fiber $H$ of $f$ consequently has diagonal $H\to H\times H$ an equivalence. If $F$ is also essentially surjective, Step 7 makes each such $H$ nonempty. Choose $h\in H$; a homotopy inverse to the diagonal gives $\mathrm{pr}_1\simeq\mathrm{pr}_2$ on $H\times H$, and restriction along $z\mapsto(z,h)$ contracts $H$ to $h$. Every fiber of $f$ is therefore contractible, so [lem-coef-space-contractible-fiber-equivalence] implies that $I(F)$ is an equivalence. If $B$ is empty, so is $A$; the same criterion is vacuous and still applies.

source.place: Proposition 5.3.6; the homotopy-monomorphism and surjectivity argument is written out using descent and contractible fibers.

proof.text: Suppose $F:C\to D$ is fully faithful and $f=U(F):X\to Y$ is an equivalence. In the total-category description of [def-coef-complete-algebroid], write $F$ as $C\xrightarrow{\alpha}f^*D\to D$. Its vertical factor $\alpha$ is a map of $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$-algebras with equivalences at all colors $(x,x')$, by full faithfulness. Since $\mathcal V$ is presentably monoidal and $\Delta_X^{\mathrm{op}}$ is small, the conservativity clause of [lem-coef-operadic-colorwise-sifted-colimits] says that $\alpha$ is an equivalence. The second factor is the Cartesian lift constructed in Step 2. For every testing algebroid $T$, its mapping-space square over $\operatorname{Map}(U(T),X)\to\operatorname{Map}(U(T),Y)$ is a homotopy pullback by the mapping-square clause of [lem-coef-cocartesian-straightening], applied to opposites. The bottom map is an equivalence, hence so is $\operatorname{Map}(T,f^*D)\to\operatorname{Map}(T,D)$. Composing with $\alpha$ gives an equivalence $\operatorname{Map}(T,C)\to\operatorname{Map}(T,D)$. At $T=D$, lift $1_D$ to $G:D\to C$, giving $FG\simeq1_D$. At $T=C$, the images of $GF$ and $1_C$ agree up to homotopy, so the mapping-space equivalence gives $GF\simeq1_C$. These homotopies exhibit $F$ as an equivalence, without completeness.

source.place: Lemma 5.3.2 and its Cartesian mapping-space criterion, equivalent to the conservativity argument of Lemma A.5.5.

proof.text: For an object equivalence $\alpha:x\to y$, Step 5 supplies a reverse arrow $\beta:y\to x$ and the two inverse homotopies. Composition and units are those of the algebroid in [def-coef-complete-algebroid]. Precomposition by $\alpha$ on $C(y,z)\to C(x,z)$ has inverse precomposition by $\beta$; associativity identifies their composites with composition by $\alpha\beta$ or $\beta\alpha$, and the inverse equations and unit homotopies identify these with identity maps of the enriched mapping objects themselves. For postcomposition, let $a:C(z,x)\to C(z,y)$ and $b:C(z,y)\to C(z,x)$ be composition with $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Associativity gives $ba\simeq(\beta\alpha)_*$ and $ab\simeq(\alpha\beta)_*$. The inverse equations $\beta\alpha\simeq1_x$ and $\alpha\beta\simeq1_y$, followed by the unit homotopies, identify these composites with $1_{C(z,x)}$ and $1_{C(z,y)}$. Thus $a$ and $b$ exhibit $C(z,x)\simeq C(z,y)$. This proves the assertion in $\mathcal V$, rather than only after applying $\operatorname{Map}(\mathbf1,-)$.

All identifications used here are induced by evaluation, precomposition with maps of finite coarse categories, the mapping-space adjunction and the canonical pullback comparisons. For an algebroid map $C\to D$, postcomposition commutes with every one of these restrictions; on an arbitrary higher simplex it is the same associative composition of the specified coherent functors. Units, composition and their homotopies are part of an algebroid map. Thus the identifications of simplicial spaces and of invertible-arrow subspaces, the fiber comparisons, and the induced augmentations commute coherently with algebroid maps. The temporary choices of enumerations or inverses in the proof establish equivalences of these canonical maps and do not enter their definitions.

source.place: Naturality of the canonical evaluation and restriction maps throughout Sections 5.1-5.3.
